Isoform switching after LPS, and what UBL5 does to it

Lab meeting update — state of the project, open decisions, and what’s next

Author

Project

Published

August 22, 2026

NoteHow to read this update

This replaces the earlier seminar summary as the current picture. It covers the whole project: the original pipeline (scripts 00–07), the layer-decoupling and hidden-layer work (08–10), and the external review round.

Three claims we previously reported are withdrawn. They are listed in Section 2 rather than quietly dropped, because two of them were headline results and one of them shaped a script. Everything still standing has been re-checked against the tables it came from.

1 Where the project stands

Two questions, tracked separately throughout because they have different answers and different levels of support.

The one-line version. Q1 is in good shape and has a real, defensible result. Q2 has a solid negative (no constitutive defect, not pathway-targeted) and a solid global phenotype (halved LPS response), but the splicing-specific claim — the reason UBL5 is interesting — is currently unresolved and blocked on a proper model-based refit.

2 What changed since the last update

ImportantThree retractions and one retirement

Each was reproducible from its table and still wrong. Reproducing one of these numbers is a check on the code, not a licence to quote it.

1. The expression-vs-splicing layer asymmetry (64% vs 38%) is retracted. This was the load-bearing evidence for a splicing-specific UBL5 role. It compares two estimators biased in opposite directions; on a calibrated scale the gap inverts. Detail and the calibration in Section 5.2. The mediation decomposition (36% / 64%) inherits the same compressed estimator and goes with it.

2. The “UT deficit does not survive its confounder” reading is withdrawn. We stratified switching rates on each gene’s own LPS-response magnitude and found the odds ratio drop from 0.51 to a non-significant MH 0.77 (p = 0.11). The arithmetic is right; the causal logic was not. UBL5 is a spliceosome-associated modifier, so if splicing regulation sits upstream of the LPS response then response magnitude is a mediator, not a confounder — and conditioning on a mediator subtracts the very effect being measured.1 The numbers stay on the record; they are not evidence the deficit is an artefact.

3. The ISG “sparing” result is withdrawn. On the relative scale, interferon-response genes looked protected in the KO (63% of response retained vs 37% transcriptome-wide). On the absolute scale the same genes lose more (Section 5.3). Conditioning on expression, LPS-responsiveness survives (p = 0.002) but ISG status does not (p = 0.27) — the interferon effect was abundance.

4. The H-vs-T switching contrast is retired, not recomputed. H_HT is the one dataset that had a batch correction applied to it, so its rates and dIF distributions are not on the same scale as the other three. Details in Section 3.1 — this one is a methods finding with consequences well beyond the single contrast.

Also superseded: the TSS bimodality (and its 2.7 kb antimode), and the alternative-first-exon percentages computed from the Ensembl subset — both replaced by full-GFF3 results in Section 4.3.

3 The data, and whether it holds up

Four datasets on two merged reference transcriptomes: Q1 (HT) is T_HT (WT THP-1 ± LPS, our anchor) with H_HT as a supplementary genotype; Q2 (UT) is T_UT (WT) versus U_UT (UBL5 KO), both ± LPS.

3.1 H_HT is not on the same scale as the others

WarningDo not read the H_HT row alongside the other three

H_HT’s 2.07% switching rate is not comparable to T_HT’s 0.87%, for two independent reasons.

It is the only batch-corrected dataset. importRdata runs sva::num.sv on every import; it found two surrogate variables for H_HT and none for the other three, so H_HT alone had limma::removeBatchEffect applied and every one of its IF/dIF values derives from the corrected matrix. That halves its replicate IF noise (0.0062 → 0.0030) — inverting its noise ranking, so the dataset that should be noisiest reads as the quietest — and drives the elevated rate.2

Its design is different in kind. T/U are one clonal line processed on a single day. H is primary macrophages from three donors, each prepped on a different day — two extra variance components, and they are perfectly confounded (one donor per day), so no analysis of this data can separate donor genotype from batch. A switching rate counts genes consistent across that dataset’s replicates, so H’s rate answers a strictly harder question than T’s. Their ratio is not a genotype effect under any modelling choice, which is why the contrast is retired rather than recomputed.

The fix for H is an explicit donor blocking factor (~ donor + condition), not detectUnwantedEffects = FALSE, which would leave real donor variation uncorrected.

3.2 Reproducibility: the same libraries, twice

T_HT and T_UT are the same six sequencing libraries quantified against two different merged transcriptomes, which makes them a technical control. Of 156 genes called switching in either, 55 are called in both — a Jaccard of 0.35.

Most disagreement is threshold-level rather than contradictory: 53 more are near-misses (|dIF| 0.10–0.15 in the reference that did not call them) and 24 fall below the gene expression floor; only 24 are clearly absent.

NoteTreat this as a reference point, not a ceiling

An earlier version of this analysis called 35% a “reproducibility ceiling”. That framing is retired: HT merges the T+H PacBio transcripts and UT merges T+U, so the two are not the same transcript space viewed twice. Part of the disagreement is genuine annotation-space difference rather than measurement noise.

4 Q1 — Splicing in the LPS response

4.1 The result: one in five switching genes is invisible to DE

This is the cleanest positive result in the project and the direct answer to “does the splicing layer see anything gene-level expression is blind to”.

In T_UT, 23 of 118 switching genes (19.5%) have |gene log2FC| < 0.25 — median 0.136, while shifting isoform fraction by a median of 0.171.3 The list is biologically pointed: IRAK3 (IRAK-M, a negative TLR regulator), SOCS4, SP1, RAB7B (TLR4 trafficking), LIG1.

Crucially, they are not preferentially artefacts: 64.7% are called switching again in the independent T_HT annotation of the same libraries, against a 59.8% baseline for all switchers.

4.2 Class B — “gene down, dominant isoform preserved”

A second, rarer pattern. Of 2,611 genes falling more than 0.3 log2, 56 (2.1%) hold or raise their baseline-dominant isoform while minor isoforms collapse (median: gene −0.362, dominant −0.04, minor −0.532; dominant IF rises 0.25 → 0.32).

Dominance is defined at baseline, not post-LPS — defining it after stimulation selects on the outcome and inflates the class.4

Reproduction, with denominators stated because they differ: of those 56, 47 are testable in T_HT and 11 reproduce as Class B there — 23.4% of the testable set, against a 0.52% base rate among all testable genes (45× enrichment, Fisher OR 78, p = 3e-16). On the conservative denominator (counting the 9 untestable as failures) it is 19.6%, a 37.5× enrichment. The reproducing genes: AMT, CD163L1, CKAP5, COQ6, DEDD2, FBXL19, HHLA3, NRF1, RBL2, RTEL1, VPS26C.

NoteCorrection on the record

An earlier draft named IRF3 and BCL7B as reproducing Class B genes and used IRF3 as the illustrative example. Both have reproduces_in_T_HT = FALSE. IRF3 remains an interesting single-reference observation and must be labelled as not reproducing across annotations.

Structurally, Class B genes are more isoform-complex than background (median 19.5 vs 13 isoforms, Wilcoxon p = 1.6e-5) while cryptic switchers are not (p = 0.53) — mechanistically sensible, since “gene falls while the dominant isoform holds” requires enough minor isoforms to absorb the decline. Class B looks like a property of complex loci, not a distinct functional programme, and at 2.1% it matters for interpreting specific genes rather than as a claim that DE is broadly misleading.

4.3 What the switching events structurally are

This matters more than it first appears. Robinson (2021) reports that roughly half of macrophage LPS splicing changes are alternative-first-exon events — promoter choice, not spliceosome catalysis. If that held here, attributing anything to a spliceosome modifier would be undercut.

The answer is: partly, but not half. 98.6% of events differ in their first exon — which is why the “it’s all first exon” impression is well founded. But under a stringent criterion (disjoint first exon and TSS > 1 kb apart), only 21.7% are pure promoter switches with no internal junction change, while 59.4% involve a genuine internal junction change. Robinson’s concern applies to about a fifth of events.

The event-class mix is unchanged in the KO (internal-splicing share 59.4% vs 51.3%, Fisher p = 0.26), so UBL5 loss does not selectively remove one event class. TSS distances are unimodal (median 12,679 bp, Hartigan dip p = 0.99).5

ImportantWording change we should adopt

If ~22% of events are pure promoter switches and much of the rest involves 5’ truncation, a substantial fraction of what the pipeline calls “isoform switching” is TSS selection. That is a real and claimable regulatory layer — it is just not a spliceosome one. The reports should stop describing it generically as “splicing”.

5 Q2 — What UBL5 is doing

5.1 No constitutive splicing defect

Comparing unstimulated cells only, the KO’s excess over replicate noise is 0.0024 — essentially nil. The positive control (two genuinely different genotypes, H vs T) gives 0.0496, about 21× larger.

So the assay detects real composition differences, and the KO at rest does not have one. Whatever UBL5 is doing is condition-dependent. This is a within-layer comparison with no cross-layer ratio, so it is untouched by the estimator problem below.

5.2 The layer asymmetry, and why it did not survive

We reported that the KO retains 64% of its expression response but only 38% of its splicing response — non-overlapping CIs, robust to an annotation-neutral subset. That looked like direct evidence for a splicing-specific role.

The two numbers come from estimators biased in opposite directions.

  • Expression response is |log2FC| between condition means — it averages three replicates before taking the absolute value, so it tracks truth almost linearly.
  • Splicing response is a total variation distance — a sum of absolute values, which does not average noise away. For signal small relative to noise, \(E|s+n| \approx E|n| + O(s^2)\), so the estimator is roughly quadratic near zero and compresses ratios toward 0.

A genotype with 60% of the true signal reads as 68% by the expression estimator and 42% by the splicing estimator. Comparing an upward-biased number to a downward-biased one manufactures an asymmetry even when both layers are reduced by exactly the same factor.

Inverting the calibration turns 64% / 38% into 53% / 57% — the observed gap of +0.26 becomes −0.04. The splicing layer is no longer the more-degraded one.

ImportantThe two corrected analyses agree on direction only — do not overstate this

The pipeline’s own estimator (observed 60% / 65%) corrects to 48% / 75%, a gap of -0.27, against the external review’s -0.04. Both corrected gaps are ≤ 0, so neither supports “splicing degrades more” — but they differ by 23 points, and the pipeline’s version implies splicing is retained ~1.6× better than expression, which the review’s does not.

The honest reading: after correction, no reliable cross-layer ordering can be extracted from either estimator. Not that both converge on parity.

Matching the estimator structure does not rescue the comparison. An identical across-minus-within pairwise form applied to both layers narrows the gap from 26 to 14 points (expression 53.7%, splicing 39.9%) but cannot close it, because compression depends on signal-to-noise, not just estimator form — and the layers differ there by 20× (WT expression SNR 1.81, splicing 0.09). At SNR 0.09 the splicing estimator is deep in the quadratic regime while expression is not.6

What this does and does not overturn. It does not show UBL5 has no splicing-specific role — it shows this measurement cannot demonstrate one in either direction. It does not touch the baseline result above, and it does not touch the globally blunted expression response, which rests on expression alone.

5.3 What the deficit is not

Not LPS-pathway-specific. If UBL5 were required for an LPS-induced splicing programme, the deficit should concentrate in LPS-responsive genes. It does the opposite on the relative scale — and that reading is the artefact:

Interferon-response genes retain 62.8% against a 36.6% transcriptome average — but they lose 0.0122 in absolute terms against 0.0081. Conditioning on expression quintiles, LPS-responsiveness stays significant (p = 0.002) while ISG status does not (p = 0.27). The interferon effect was abundance. Report both scales or neither.

No network proximity to TLR4. Using the full STRING v12 human physical interactome (15,809 proteins, 210,667 edges at score ≥ 400) seeded with 33 TLR4-pathway proteins and tested against a degree-matched null, every candidate set is non-significant: switching in WT p = 0.49, KO p = 0.18, UBL5-dependent p = 0.69, cryptic p = 0.56, Class B p = 0.26.

The reason is structural and visible in the null itself — degree-matched random genes sit only 2.20–2.47 steps from the pathway (SD 0.10–0.24). In a network this dense, almost every expressed gene is two to three steps from TLR4, so distance carries almost no discriminating information.7

5.4 What survives on the positive side

Two results from the network work do stand:

  • A short list of candidates that are genuine direct physical interactors of pathway components (direct_TLR4_interactors.csv).
  • UBL5’s own neighbourhood: 62% of its 82 partners are core spliceosome or RBP, including a direct SART1 edge — the mammalian counterpart of the known Hub1–Snu66 interaction. Its single apparent TLR4 link is to UBE2N and is best read as ubiquitin-system co-annotation, not signalling.

This is suggestive of a spliceosomal role, but it is annotation, not measurement from our data. It cannot substitute for the refit.

6 Candidates for validation

6.1 Q1 candidates — two lists, two questions

The candidate set carried through the external review (IRAK3, SOCS4, RAB7B, SPRING1) is Q2-shaped. Its chain is: 117 switching genes in T_UT → 23 cryptic → 4 genes hand-picked for TLR-pathway relevance → 7 isoforms. Their ranks among the 23 cryptic switchers are 1, 3, 10 and 11, so this is a judgement call for assay design, not a statistical selection — no claim of the form “the top candidates are TLR genes” follows from it.

Two gaps followed, and scripts/11_q1_candidates.R now fills them. The set never used T_HT, the designated Q1 anchor; and the cryptic filter, while exactly right for the sub-question, discards the largest switches in the data purely because those genes also change in abundance.

NoteWhy these are two lists rather than one ranked table with a flag

“Invisible to DE” is a sub-question within Q1, not the main one, so it gets its own list. A gene can be a strong answer to one and irrelevant to the other. Ranking the response list by effect and then filtering it to cryptic would bury the point of the cryptic list, where membership is the finding and rank is secondary.

6.1.1 List A — the wildtype LPS response

The main Q1 question, ranked purely by effect size.

A coherent interferon and inflammatory signature — NCOA7, RSAD2, DDX58, IFITM2, IL23A, CCL3, CD86, KDM6B, GBP1 — and almost entirely disjoint from the Q2 four.

6.1.2 List B — switches differential expression would miss

The sub-question, and the one the hidden-layer analysis is about. 37 genes qualify; 8 are annotation-robust.

WarningTwo things this table is careful about

Failing annotation-robustness has two different causes. A gene tested in the other annotation and not called is a real disagreement; a gene below the expression floor there was never given the chance. IRAK3 is the worked example — gene expression 10.3 in T_HT against a floor of 12 — so its absence from the anchor is missing data, not evidence against it. The annotation_status column keeps these apart.

T_HT/T_UT agreement is robustness to transcript space, not replication. Same six libraries, same RNA. H_HT agreement is genuine cross-genotype support, but it is reported as a flag only and never used as a filter, since H_HT alone is batch-corrected (Section 3.1). No H_HT effect size is compared to a T effect size anywhere.

ImportantNeither Q1 list has been through the assayability screen yet

The nesting and primer-specificity analysis that eliminated 6 of the 7 Q2 candidates below has not been run on these genes. Expect it to remove several. Until it has, treat both lists as biological shortlists, not assay-ready ones. This is the next task — see Section 9.

6.2 Q2 candidates and assay feasibility

WarningMost of these cannot be assayed by qPCR, for a structural reason

Of 7 candidate isoforms, 5 are fully nested inside a longer isoform — every junction and every base they contain is also present in the host transcript, so no primer pair can distinguish them. A 6th (SOCS4 TCONS_00086549) is not nested but still has zero unique sequence ≥ 60 bp, because other isoforms tile across all of it.

That leaves one designable assay: the IRAK3 long form TCONS_00065141 — 129 bp product, specificity verified empirically as 1 of 315,349 transcripts by matching both primers against every transcript in fa/transcripts_U-T.fa, not predicted.

The right assays instead: the discriminating feature for the nested isoforms is the 5’ end (TSS 863 bp to 55.8 kb apart), so 5’ RACE, CAGE, or targeted long-read cDNA. Long-read cDNA on the validation RNA would resolve all seven at once and is likely cheaper than developing six assays that cannot work.

7 Methods notes worth carrying forward

Short version of the traps this project has actually fallen into. Full treatment in docs/STATISTICAL_METHODS.md.

Backgrounds. Every enrichment test uses the genes quantified and tested in that same experiment (8,000–12,000 per dataset), recovered from unfiltered exports. Never the whole genome, and never the saved analysis objects — those were written with reduceToSwitchingGenes = TRUE, so every gene in them is already significant. One early test in this project had a background of 25 genes, all significant by construction, and reported an odds ratio of 15.

The abundance floor. min_gene_expression = 12, derived from replicate IF noise versus gene expression. dIF is a ratio, so at low gene abundance the isoform fraction rests on few reads. It removes 33–52% of raw calls by design, and is_switching_before_expr_floor is kept so the cost stays auditable.8

Effect sizes over p-values. With thousands of matched isoforms, p-values track n. A paired Wilcoxon p of 7e-9 on a median log2 ratio of 0.003 is sample size, not biology.

Calibrate before comparing layers. The general lesson from Section 5.2: any claim of the form “layer X is affected more than layer Y” needs its estimators calibrated first. The results in Section 4 and Section 5.3 do not have this problem — they are within-layer comparisons, proportions, or structural classifications.

The measurement ceiling on all of this. Everything above derives from ISA’s condition means and replicate isoform fractions. The composition measure is a reasonable summary but is not a formal differential-splicing test, and Section 5.2 is the concrete cost of that.

8 Where we need your input

These are blocking or near-blocking, and we cannot resolve them from the data.

1. What exactly is the UBL5 allele? Full knockout, frameshift, hypomorph, degron, or knockdown? Published work reports human UBL5 as essential for viability (Ammon et al. 2014), so a viable complete null needs explaining. If it is a hypomorph or partial knockdown that changes the interpretation substantially and reconciles a literature contradiction. This is the cheapest thing on the list and its outcome reframes everything else.

2. Library chemistry — polyA-selected or ribo-depleted? Intron retention is the readout most diagnostic for a Hub1/UBL5 mechanism, and it is poorly captured by polyA selection. If the existing libraries are polyA, the central falsification test needs new sequencing.

3. LPS dose, timepoint, and PMA differentiation protocol. Needed so any validation experiment matches the original conditions.

4. Do we want the count scale decision made now? For the refit (Section 9) we must choose between ISA’s scaledTPM — the recommended scale for DTU, since raw expected counts are biased by effective-length differences between isoforms of the same gene — and RSEM expected counts. They differ per-isoform by 0.18–2.3×. Both are derivable from the supplied files. Default recommendation is scaledTPM, but it should be a deliberate, recorded choice.

5. Is the TSS reframing acceptable? Given Section 4.3, should we retitle this work from “isoform switching” to something that leads with promoter/TSS selection? It is more accurate and arguably a cleaner story, but it changes the framing of the whole project.

9 What’s planned next

Ordered by what would change a conclusion.

1. Model-based refit from raw counts — the blocking step. This is now unblocked: RSEM matrices for all twelve libraries per reference arrived and every ISA object has been reconciled against them. Because the UT file carries all twelve, the layer question becomes a genotype × treatment interaction in one 2×2 model rather than a comparison of two separately-fit runs — which removes the cross-run normalisation problem and the estimator problem in Section 5.2 at the same time.

Plan: satuRn or DEXSeq, with the pairing included and an explicit blocking factor (~ donor + condition for H, ~ replicate + condition for T/U), re-imported under a single ISA version.9 Until this runs, the splicing-specific UBL5 claim stays unresolved.

2. Run the assayability screen on the Q1 lists. The nesting and primer-specificity analysis that eliminated 6 of the 7 Q2 candidates has not been applied to List A or List B (Section 6.1). Everything it needs is on disk — gff3/U_T.gff3 and fa/transcripts_U-T.fa — so it runs without the external drive. Expect it to remove several candidates, and expect the 5′-end problem to recur: if ~22% of events are pure promoter switches (Section 4.3), nested isoforms are the norm rather than the exception here.

3. Recompute the mediation decomposition on a calibrated scale. It inherits the compressed estimator and is currently unquotable.

4. Promote the hidden-layer analysis into the pipeline. scripts/03b_hidden_layer.R writing per-dataset cryptic-switcher and Class B tables with cross-annotation reproduction flags, so these stop living only in the review tree.

5. GO enrichment on the hidden-layer sets. Could not be run during the review — Bioconductor mirrors were unreachable from that sandbox. gene_sets/ has everything needed (universe_tested_genes.txt, 8,916 symbols, plus the four candidate sets); feed them through 05_pathway_enrichment.R so the universe convention matches the rest of the project. At 11–56 genes this is likely underpowered, so a more informative alternative is to annotate the isoforms instead — are the lost minor isoforms NMD targets or truncated, and the retained dominant ones full-length coding? That converts “purification” from a pattern into a mechanism.

6. Re-examine the abundance floor under a paired noise model. The floor was derived from within-condition replicate IF noise without using the pairing; a paired estimate should be smaller and would recover some of the 33–52% of calls currently removed. Do this after the re-import, not before.

7. Wet-lab sequence (full proposal, ordered cheapest-potentially-fatal-first, in docs/external_review/EXPERIMENTS.md): allele characterisation → intron retention under stimulation, ribo-depleted → the IRAK3 assay → independent perturbation as a clonal-artefact control → rescue, only once the first three support the model.

10 Appendix — provenance

Every table in results/ carries a run_manifest.json entry recording the git SHA, R version, package versions and thresholds that produced it. Reports are read-only consumers of those tables.

Standing caveats. The four ISA objects are pre-reduced to switching genes, so “genes present” ≠ “genes tested”; significance always comes from the unfiltered context layer, never from the reduced objects. TCONS_* ids are assigned per reference and are not comparable across HT and UT — cross-reference comparisons join on gene symbols.

ImportantInputs are already reduced to switching genes

All 4 of 4 input ISA objects contain only genes that already pass the gene-level q cutoff (saved after isoformSwitchTestDEXSeq(reduceToSwitchingGenes = TRUE)).

Consequences for everything below: gene counts are genes retained, not genes tested; “present in the other dataset” means retained in that saved object, not tested and non-significant; and any percentage of genes has a denominator that was already selected on the outcome. Overlap between datasets is bounded by how many symbols survive in both objects. No enrichment test against this background is reported. See docs/REVIEW_CHANGES.md.
